overview: SCD Type 3 (Slowly Changing Dimension Type 3) is a technique for tracking a LIMITED amount of history in a dimension table by adding extra columns rather than inserting new rows.
When a tracked attribute changes, the existing value is shifted into a 'previous' column and the new value is written into the 'current' column, keeping the row count unchanged.
It is ideal when only the most recent prior value (or a small fixed number of prior values) is needed for comparison, and full historical lineage is unnecessary.
learningObjectives: Understand how SCD Type 3 stores limited history using additional columns instead of new rows.
Learn the UPDATE mechanics that shift the current value to a previous column when an attribute changes.
Identify when Type 3 is appropriate versus Type 1 (overwrite) and Type 2 (full history).
coreConcept.formalDefinition: SCD Type 3 is a dimension-management pattern in which a fixed number of prior values of a changing attribute are preserved in dedicated columns (e.g., current_region and previous_region), optionally accompanied by an effective_date marking when the change occurred. Each natural key maps to exactly one dimension row; on change, values cascade across the columns and the oldest retained value is discarded.
coreConcept.simpleExplanation: Imagine a customer moves from the 'West' sales region to the 'East' region. Instead of creating a brand-new row for the customer (Type 2) or simply overwriting the old region and forgetting it (Type 1), Type 3 keeps both: it puts 'East' in the current_region column and 'West' in the previous_region column on the same row. You can now compare 'before and after' instantly, but if the customer moves again, the very first region is lost.
coreConcept.historicalContext: The Slowly Changing Dimension taxonomy was formalized by Ralph Kimball as part of dimensional modeling for data warehouses in the 1990s. Type 3 was introduced for the specific case of organizational realignments (e.g., resegmenting sales territories) where analysts needed to view facts under both the old and new groupings simultaneously, without the storage or query complexity of full Type 2 history.

whyItMatters.business: Enables 'as-was vs as-is' comparison reporting (e.g., sales by old region vs new region) immediately after a reorganization, supporting realignment analysis and smooth transitions without rebuilding historical reports.
whyItMatters.engineering: Provides a lightweight history mechanism with constant row counts, simpler ETL than Type 2, and trivial query patterns since both values live on the same row, avoiding window functions or effective-date range joins.
whyItMatters.scalability: Because no new rows are added on change, the dimension stays compact and joins to large fact tables remain fast and predictable, which matters when the dimension is hit by billions of fact rows.
whyItMatters.cost: Minimizes storage growth (no row explosion) and reduces compute on queries by eliminating the need for date-range filtering, lowering warehouse credit/compute consumption.
whyItMatters.reliability: With a single row per natural key, surrogate-key reuse and 'point-in-time' join correctness are simpler to reason about, reducing the class of bugs caused by selecting the wrong version of a Type 2 row.

coreComponents.name: Current Attribute Column
coreComponents.definition: The column that always holds the most recent value of the tracked attribute.
coreComponents.purpose: To serve the present-day value for the dimension member.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Updated to the incoming value whenever a change is detected.

coreComponents.name: Previous Attribute Column(s)
coreComponents.definition: One or more columns that retain the immediately prior value(s) of the tracked attribute.
coreComponents.purpose: To preserve limited history for before/after comparison.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Receives the value being displaced from the current column on each change; oldest retained value is dropped.

coreComponents.name: Effective Date Column
coreComponents.definition: A date/timestamp column recording when the most recent change to the tracked attribute occurred.
coreComponents.purpose: To provide context on when the current value took effect.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Set to the change date during the UPDATE; helps disambiguate the period each value applies to.

internalWorking: On each ETL load, the incoming (staged) value for the tracked attribute is compared against the current_<attribute> column for the matching natural key.
If the values are identical, no change is applied (the row is left untouched, or only non-tracked Type 1 attributes are overwritten).
If the values differ, the existing current value is copied into the previous_<attribute> column, the new value is written into current_<attribute>, and the effective_date is set to the change date.
Because the displaced value overwrites whatever was in the previous column, any history older than the retained N values is permanently lost.
New natural keys not yet in the dimension are inserted with the current value populated and the previous column left NULL (no prior value exists).
coreConcept.architectureFlow: Source/Staging (new attribute value) -> Compare to current_<attr> -> If changed: current_<attr> -> previous_<attr>, new value -> current_<attr>, set effective_date -> Dimension row updated in place
dataFlowWalkthrough: 1. Staging load brings customer C100 with region = 'East'; the dimension currently has C100 with current_region = 'West', previous_region = NULL.
2. ETL matches on natural key cust_nk = 'C100' and compares staged region ('East') to current_region ('West').
3. Values differ, so the process shifts: previous_region is set to 'West' (the old current value).
4. current_region is updated to 'East' and region_effective_date is set to the load/change date (e.g., 2026-06-18).
5. A later load brings region = 'North' for C100; previous_region becomes 'East', current_region becomes 'North' — and the original 'West' value is now lost forever.

keyTerminology.meaning: A dimension whose attribute values change occasionally over time and for which the warehouse must decide how to handle those changes.
keyTerminology.importance: Defines the broader problem space; Type 3 is one strategy among Types 0-6.

keyTerminology.meaning: Retention of only a fixed, small number of prior attribute values (typically one) rather than the complete change log.
keyTerminology.importance: It is the defining characteristic that separates Type 3 from the unbounded history of Type 2.

keyTerminology.meaning: The ability to analyze facts under both the old and new value of an attribute at the same time using the current and previous columns.
keyTerminology.importance: This is the primary analytical motivation for choosing Type 3 over Type 1.

importantConcepts.explanation: On change, values cascade from current to previous (and, in multi-level Type 3, previous to previous-previous). The new value enters current and the oldest retained value falls off the end and is discarded. This keeps history bounded by the number of columns provisioned.

The amount of history Type 3 can hold is fixed at design time by the number of columns. Adding history depth, or tracking a new attribute's prior value, requires a DDL schema change (ALTER TABLE) and ETL changes — unlike Type 2 where depth is unbounded automatically.

variationsAndTypes: **Single-Previous-Value Type 3:** The classic form — one current_<attr> and one previous_<attr> column, retaining exactly one prior value.
**Multi-Level Type 3:** Several prior-value columns (e.g., current, previous, two-periods-ago) to retain a fixed N>1 history; values cascade across all columns on change.

**Hybrid Type 6 (1+2+3):** Combines Type 1 (current value overwrite), Type 2 (new row per change for full history), and Type 3 (a current_value column on every historical row), giving both full history and easy current-vs-historical comparison on each row.
advantages: **Constant Row Count:** No new rows are created on change, so the dimension stays small and fact-table joins remain fast and predictable.
**Simple Queries:** Both the current and prior values sit on the same row, so before/after comparisons need no window functions or effective-date range joins.
**Dual-Grouping Analysis:** Lets analysts report facts under both the old and new attribute value simultaneously — ideal for organizational realignments.
**Low Storage and Compute Cost:** Minimal storage growth and cheaper query plans than Type 2, reducing warehouse spend.
disadvantages: **Lossy History:** Only a fixed number of prior values are kept; older changes are permanently overwritten and unrecoverable.
**Schema Rigidity:** Increasing history depth or tracking another attribute's prior value requires DDL/ETL changes, not just more rows.
**Poor Fit for Frequent Change:** Attributes that change often render the single previous column nearly useless and lose intermediate states.
**No Full Audit Trail:** Cannot satisfy compliance/audit requirements that demand complete point-in-time history of every change.

tradeOffs.whenToUse: Use Type 3 when only the immediately prior value matters (e.g., current vs previous sales region/territory), when an organizational realignment requires dual-grouping comparison, and when full Type 2 history would be overkill or too costly.
tradeOffs.whenToAvoid: Avoid Type 3 when complete historical lineage or audit trails are required, when the attribute changes frequently, or when you need point-in-time fact attribution to many historical states — use Type 2 instead.

coreConcept.realWorldAnalogy: Think of a contact card that has a 'Current Address' line and a single 'Previous Address' line. When someone moves, you erase the previous-address line, copy the old current address down into it, and write the new address on the current line. You always know where they live now and where they lived just before — but the address from two moves ago is gone, because there is only one slot for history.

commonMisconceptions.myth: SCD Type 3 keeps the full history of an attribute, just in columns instead of rows.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Type 3 keeps only a fixed number of prior values (usually one). Every change overwrites the oldest retained value, so it is inherently lossy — it is NOT a column-based equivalent of Type 2.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Type 3 is just a worse version of Type 2 and should always be avoided.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Type 3 is purpose-built for limited before/after comparison with constant row counts and simple queries. For realignment analysis where only the prior value matters, it is simpler and cheaper than Type 2.

productionConsiderations.scalability: Row counts stay flat regardless of how often attributes change, so the dimension scales gracefully and joins to massive fact tables stay performant; the cost is bounded, lossy history.
productionConsiderations.reliability: One row per natural key means deterministic joins and no risk of selecting the wrong version, but reliability of historical reporting is limited by the fixed retention depth.
productionConsiderations.faultTolerance: Idempotent UPDATE logic must guard against re-shifting columns when a load is replayed; compare staged-vs-current before shifting so a re-run does not push an unchanged value into the previous column.
productionConsiderations.monitoring: Track the rate of attribute changes per natural key; a high change rate signals the single previous column is losing meaningful history and the attribute may need Type 2.
productionConsiderations.security: Previous-value columns may expose historical PII (e.g., prior address); apply the same masking/access controls as the current value and consider retention policies.
productionConsiderations.costOptimization: Avoids row explosion and date-range query overhead, lowering storage and compute; provision only as many previous columns as analysts genuinely use to avoid wasted width.
productionConsiderations.performance: Updating a fixed set of columns in place is cheap; ensure the natural key is indexed for the merge/lookup, and prefer set-based MERGE/UPDATE over row-by-row processing.

codeExamples.title: Creating an SCD Type 3 Dimension Table
codeExamples.overview: Defines a customer dimension that tracks the current and one previous sales region, plus the date the current region took effect.
codeExamples.code:
CREATE TABLE dim_customer (
    customer_sk        INT PRIMARY KEY,          -- surrogate key
    customer_nk        VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL,     -- natural/business key
    customer_name      VARCHAR(100),
    current_region     VARCHAR(50),              -- most recent value
    previous_region    VARCHAR(50),              -- one prior value (NULL if never changed)
    region_effective_date DATE,                  -- when current_region took effect
    CONSTRAINT uq_customer_nk UNIQUE (customer_nk)
);
codeExamples.breakdown: customer_sk is the surrogate key; customer_nk is the business key used to match incoming records. The Type 3 history is captured by the current_region / previous_region pair, and region_effective_date records when the latest change happened. There is exactly one row per customer_nk.
codeExamples.expectedOutput: A dim_customer table with a single row per customer that can store the present region and exactly one prior region.
codeExamples.commonIssues: Forgetting the UNIQUE constraint on customer_nk allows duplicate rows per customer, breaking the single-row-per-key assumption that Type 3 relies on.
codeExamples.optimizationTips: Index/uniquely constrain customer_nk so the change-detection lookup during ETL is a fast index seek rather than a scan.

codeExamples.title: Applying a Change: Shift Current to Previous
codeExamples.overview: When a customer's region changes, this UPDATE moves the old current_region into previous_region and writes the new value into current_region.
codeExamples.code:
-- stg_customer holds the incoming/latest values
UPDATE d
SET previous_region        = d.current_region,   -- shift old current down
    current_region         = s.region,            -- write new current
    region_effective_date  = CURRENT_DATE
FROM dim_customer AS d
JOIN stg_customer AS s
  ON d.customer_nk = s.customer_nk
WHERE d.current_region IS DISTINCT FROM s.region;  -- only when it actually changed

-- insert brand-new customers (no prior value yet)
INSERT INTO dim_customer (customer_sk, customer_nk, customer_name, current_region, previous_region, region_effective_date)
SELECT nextval('customer_sk_seq'), s.customer_nk, s.customer_name, s.region, NULL, CURRENT_DATE
FROM stg_customer AS s
LEFT JOIN dim_customer AS d ON d.customer_nk = s.customer_nk
WHERE d.customer_nk IS NULL;
codeExamples.breakdown: The UPDATE fires only when current_region differs from the staged region (IS DISTINCT FROM handles NULLs safely). The assignment order matters logically: previous_region takes the OLD current_region value, while current_region takes the new staged value. New customers are inserted with previous_region = NULL because no prior value exists.
codeExamples.expectedOutput: Changed customers have their prior region preserved in previous_region and the new region in current_region; unchanged customers are untouched; new customers are inserted.
codeExamples.commonIssues: Omitting the IS DISTINCT FROM guard re-shifts unchanged rows on every load, destroying the genuine previous value. Reversing the SET assignments would overwrite the old value before it is captured.
codeExamples.optimizationTips: Use a single set-based MERGE/UPDATE+INSERT instead of row-by-row logic; ensure the load is idempotent so replays do not corrupt the previous column.

codeExamples.title: Hybrid Type 3 (Type 1 + Type 3) Reporting Query
codeExamples.overview: A query that uses the current and previous columns to compare a metric under both the old and new region grouping simultaneously.
codeExamples.code:
SELECT
    d.current_region,
    d.previous_region,
    SUM(f.sales_amount)                              AS sales_current_grouping,
    SUM(CASE WHEN d.previous_region IS NOT NULL
             THEN f.sales_amount ELSE 0 END)         AS sales_attributable_to_prior
FROM fact_sales AS f
JOIN dim_customer AS d
  ON f.customer_sk = d.customer_sk
GROUP BY d.current_region, d.previous_region
ORDER BY d.current_region;
codeExamples.breakdown: Because both current_region and previous_region live on the same dimension row, a single join to the fact table lets analysts roll up sales under the new region while still seeing what region those customers previously belonged to — no effective-date range join or window function needed.
codeExamples.expectedOutput: A result set showing sales grouped by the new region alongside the prior region label, enabling before/after realignment comparison.
codeExamples.commonIssues: Analysts may wrongly assume previous_region reflects history at the time each fact occurred — it only reflects the single most recent prior value, not point-in-time state.
codeExamples.optimizationTips: For true point-in-time attribution across many historical states, this pattern is insufficient; use a Type 2 dimension instead.

endToEndExample.businessProblem: A retail company reorganizes its sales territories. Leadership wants to compare each customer's sales under the new territory grouping against their old grouping for one transition quarter, without rebuilding all historical reports or maintaining full row-level history.
endToEndExample.inputData: Daily staging extract of customers (customer_nk, customer_name, region) from the CRM, and a fact_sales table keyed by customer_sk with sales_amount and sale_date.
endToEndExample.architecture: A dimensional warehouse (e.g., Snowflake/Redshift/PostgreSQL) with a Type 3 dim_customer holding current_region, previous_region, and region_effective_date, joined to a large fact_sales table on the surrogate key.
processingSteps: 1. Land the daily CRM extract into stg_customer.
2. For existing customers, compare staged region to current_region (IS DISTINCT FROM).
3. Where different, shift current_region into previous_region, set current_region to the new value, and set region_effective_date.
4. Insert any new customers with previous_region = NULL.
5. Run comparison reports grouping fact_sales by current_region and previous_region.
endToEndExample.output: A dim_customer where realigned customers carry both their new and immediately prior region on one row, plus reports that show sales under both groupings for the transition period.
endToEndExample.monitoring: Monitor the count of region changes per load; an unexpected spike may indicate a bad CRM extract that would wrongly shift the previous column for many customers.
endToEndExample.errorHandling: Guard the UPDATE with IS DISTINCT FROM so replays/duplicate loads do not re-shift unchanged rows; wrap the load in a transaction so a failure rolls back rather than leaving columns half-shifted.
endToEndExample.finalResult: The business gets immediate before/after realignment analysis with a compact, fast dimension; the trade-off is that only the single prior region is retained — territory assignments older than one change are not available.

industryUseCases.problem: Sales territories are redrawn and leadership needs to compare performance under the old vs new territory definitions during the transition.
industryUseCases.solution: A Type 3 dim_sales_rep / dim_customer with current_territory and previous_territory columns lets reports group facts under both definitions from a single row.
industryUseCases.benefits: Instant dual-grouping comparison, no report rebuild, compact dimension, and simple queries during the realignment period.

industryUseCases.problem: Customers are re-segmented (e.g., from 'Retail' to 'Wealth') and analysts want to see balances/revenue under both the current and immediately prior segment.
industryUseCases.solution: Type 3 columns current_segment and previous_segment on the customer dimension capture the latest reclassification for comparison.
industryUseCases.benefits: Enables before/after segment migration analysis without full historical versioning, keeping the dimension small for fast aggregation.

industryUseCases.company: HR / Workforce Analytics (department or manager change)
industryUseCases.problem: Employees move departments and HR wants to compare headcount or cost between an employee's current and prior department for transition reporting.
industryUseCases.solution: An employee dimension with current_department and previous_department columns plus a dept_effective_date tracks the latest move.
industryUseCases.benefits: Lightweight tracking of the most recent organizational change, supporting transition dashboards without the storage cost of full Type 2 history.

productionDeepDive.scalability: Because changes update columns in place, the dimension does not grow with change frequency, keeping it small and joins to billion-row fact tables fast. The scalability ceiling is analytical, not physical: retention depth is fixed by column count.
productionDeepDive.faultTolerance: Loads must be idempotent. Always compare staged-vs-current before shifting columns so a replayed or duplicated load does not push an unchanged value into the previous column and silently corrupt history.
productionDeepDive.highAvailability: The single-row-per-key model simplifies replication and avoids the version-selection ambiguity of Type 2, so read replicas serve consistent current/previous values without effective-date logic.
productionDeepDive.disasterRecovery: Since older history is intentionally discarded, point-in-time recovery cannot reconstruct values beyond the retained previous columns; if richer recovery is needed, persist source change events separately or use Type 2.
productionDeepDive.performanceOptimization: Index/cluster on the natural key for fast change-detection lookups, use set-based MERGE/UPDATE rather than row-by-row, and keep the number of previous columns minimal to reduce row width.
productionDeepDive.costOptimization: Avoids the storage and compute blow-up of row-versioned Type 2 and removes the need for date-range filtering in queries, lowering warehouse credits; provision previous columns only for attributes analysts actually compare.
productionDeepDive.securityConsiderations: Previous-value columns can retain sensitive historical data (e.g., prior address, prior salary band). Apply identical masking, column-level security, and retention policies to previous columns as to their current counterparts.
productionDeepDive.monitoringAndObservability: Alert on the per-load change rate and on rows where previous_region equals current_region (a sign of erroneous re-shifting). Track how often the prior column is actually queried to validate the design choice.
productionDeepDive.dataQualityValidation: Validate that exactly one row exists per natural key, that previous != current after a genuine change, and that effective_date is non-decreasing across loads for a given key.
productionDeepDive.loggingAndAlerting: Log every change event (key, old value, new value, date) to an audit/CDC sink so that even though Type 3 discards deep history, a separate immutable log preserves it for compliance if ever needed.

recommendedPractices: **Guard changes with IS DISTINCT FROM:** Only shift columns when the staged value genuinely differs from the current value to keep loads idempotent.
**Add an effective_date:** Record when the current value took effect so the prior value has temporal context.
**Reserve Type 3 for low-frequency, comparison-driven attributes:** Use it where only the immediately prior value matters (e.g., realignments).
**Persist a separate change log:** Stream change events to an audit table so deep history is not permanently lost even though the dimension discards it.
engineeringStandards: Enforce a UNIQUE/PK constraint on the natural key so there is exactly one row per dimension member.
Use set-based MERGE/UPDATE+INSERT operations rather than row-by-row processing for change application.
Make the entire load transactional and idempotent so partial or replayed runs cannot leave columns half-shifted.
designRecommendations: Provision only as many previous columns as analysts will actually use to avoid unnecessary row width.
Name columns clearly with current_/previous_ prefixes so the temporal meaning is self-documenting.
Plan for graduation to Type 2 (or hybrid Type 6) up front if there is any chance full history will later be required.
namingConventions: Prefix tracked columns with their temporal role: current_<attr>, previous_<attr>, and where N>1, <attr>_2_periods_ago.
Name the date column <attr>_effective_date to indicate it marks when the current value took effect.
documentationStandards: Document which attributes are Type 3 and how many prior values are retained.
State explicitly that history older than the retained columns is discarded so consumers do not assume full lineage.
Record the effective_date semantics (date of change, not date of fact).
testingStrategies: Test that a genuine change correctly shifts current to previous and writes the new current value.
Test idempotency: re-running the same load must NOT alter previous_region for unchanged rows.
Test that new natural keys are inserted with previous_<attr> = NULL and that a second change discards the original value as expected.

commonMistakes.mistake: Re-shifting columns on every load regardless of whether the value changed.
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: The change-detection predicate (IS DISTINCT FROM) is omitted, so the UPDATE always copies current into previous.
commonMistakes.impact: The genuine prior value is overwritten with the current value on every run, so previous_<attr> ends up equal to current_<attr> and real history is destroyed.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Only fire the column shift when the staged value differs from the current value, and make the load idempotent.

commonMistakes.mistake: Choosing Type 3 for an attribute that changes frequently.
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Type 3 looks cheaper than Type 2, so it gets applied uniformly without considering change velocity.
commonMistakes.impact: A single previous column is constantly overwritten, losing all but the most recent change; intermediate states needed for analysis vanish.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Reserve Type 3 for low-frequency, comparison-driven attributes; use Type 2 for frequently changing attributes that need full history.

commonMistakes.mistake: Assuming previous_<attr> represents point-in-time history for fact attribution.
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Analysts treat the previous column like Type 2 versioning and expect each fact to map to the value that was current when it occurred.
commonMistakes.impact: Reports misattribute historical facts because the previous column only holds the single most recent prior value, not the value in effect at each fact's date.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Use Type 3 only for current-vs-previous comparison; for accurate point-in-time fact attribution, model the attribute as Type 2.

comparisonSection.explanation: Type 2 stores unlimited history by inserting a new versioned row per change (with effective/expiry dates and a current flag), growing the row count over time. Type 3 stores only a fixed number of prior values in additional columns on the same row, keeping the row count constant but discarding older history. Type 2 supports point-in-time fact attribution and full audit; Type 3 supports only simple current-vs-previous comparison.

Type 1 simply overwrites the old value with the new one, keeping no history at all and offering the simplest query. Type 3 also keeps a single row but preserves the immediately prior value in a separate column, enabling before/after comparison that Type 1 cannot. Both keep constant row counts and avoid date-range joins, but Type 3 trades a little extra width for limited history while Type 1 retains none.

beginnerQuestions.question: What is SCD Type 3 and how does it differ from Type 1?
beginnerQuestions.answer: SCD Type 3 tracks limited history by adding extra columns (e.g., current_region and previous_region) so the prior value is preserved on the same row. Type 1 simply overwrites the old value and keeps no history at all. Both keep one row per dimension member, but Type 3 retains the immediately prior value for comparison.
beginnerQuestions.explanation: Emphasize that Type 3 adds columns (not rows) and keeps a fixed amount of history, whereas Type 1 discards everything but the latest value.

beginnerQuestions.question: Does SCD Type 3 add new rows when an attribute changes?
beginnerQuestions.answer: No. Type 3 keeps exactly one row per natural key. On change, it shifts the old current value into a previous column and writes the new value into the current column, so the row count stays constant.
beginnerQuestions.explanation: This is the key distinction from Type 2, which inserts a new row per change.

intermediateQuestions.question: Walk through the UPDATE logic that applies a change in an SCD Type 3 dimension.
intermediateQuestions.answer: Match the staged record to the dimension on the natural key. If the staged value differs from current_<attr> (use IS DISTINCT FROM to handle NULLs), set previous_<attr> = the old current_<attr>, set current_<attr> = the new staged value, and set the effective_date. New keys are inserted with previous_<attr> = NULL.
intermediateQuestions.explanation: Stress the change-detection guard and the correct assignment order so the old value is captured before being overwritten.

intermediateQuestions.question: When would you choose Type 3 over Type 2?
intermediateQuestions.answer: Choose Type 3 when only the immediately prior value matters — for example, comparing a customer's current vs previous sales region after a territory realignment — and when full history would be overkill. Type 3 keeps the dimension compact, queries simple, and supports dual-grouping analysis from a single row.
intermediateQuestions.explanation: Tie the choice to the analytical need (limited before/after comparison) and the cost/simplicity benefits.

intermediateQuestions.question: What are the main limitations of SCD Type 3?
intermediateQuestions.answer: It retains only a fixed number of prior values, so older history is permanently lost; increasing history depth or tracking another attribute's prior value requires a schema change; it is a poor fit for frequently changing attributes; and it cannot provide a full audit trail or point-in-time fact attribution.
intermediateQuestions.explanation: Show awareness that Type 3 is inherently lossy and schema-rigid, which interviewers want to hear.

advancedQuestions.question: How would you make an SCD Type 3 load idempotent and fault-tolerant?
advancedQuestions.answer: Guard the column shift with a change-detection predicate (IS DISTINCT FROM) so unchanged rows are never re-shifted, run the load inside a transaction so failures roll back rather than leaving columns half-updated, and key change detection on staged-vs-current rather than blindly copying. Optionally log change events to a separate immutable sink for recovery.
advancedQuestions.explanation: Demonstrate understanding that re-shifting unchanged rows is the classic Type 3 corruption bug and that idempotency prevents it.

advancedQuestions.question: Explain hybrid Type 6 and how it relates to Type 3.
advancedQuestions.answer: Type 6 (1+2+3) combines all three: Type 2 gives full row-level history per change, Type 1 keeps a current-value column overwritten on every historical row, and Type 3-style current-vs-prior columns allow easy comparison on each row. It delivers full history (from Type 2) plus the simple current-vs-historical comparison that Type 3 alone provides — at the cost of more complex ETL.
advancedQuestions.explanation: Show that Type 3's comparison benefit can be folded into a richer model when full history is also required.

scenarioBasedQuestions.scenario: Your company is realigning sales territories. Leadership wants to compare each customer's sales under both the old and new territory for one transition quarter, but does not need full historical territory tracking. How do you model the customer dimension?
scenarioBasedQuestions.thinkingProcess: Identify that only the immediately prior value is needed and full history is explicitly not required — this is the textbook Type 3 case. Add current_territory and previous_territory columns plus an effective_date. On change, shift current into previous and write the new value. Reports group facts by both columns from a single row.
scenarioBasedQuestions.expectedAnswer: Model dim_customer with current_territory, previous_territory, and territory_effective_date. Apply Type 3 change logic guarded by IS DISTINCT FROM. Queries join fact_sales to the dimension once and group by both current_territory and previous_territory to compare the two groupings — no Type 2 row versioning needed.

systemDesignQuestions.problemStatement: Design the dimension strategy for a customer dimension where the country code rarely changes and only current-vs-previous comparison is needed, while the loyalty tier changes frequently and requires full history. How do you apply SCD types?
systemDesignQuestions.designApproach: Apply Type 3 to country_code (current_country, previous_country, country_effective_date) since only the prior value matters and changes are rare. Apply Type 2 to loyalty_tier using a separate versioned dimension or a Type 6 design, with effective/expiry dates and a current flag, because full history and point-in-time attribution are required.
systemDesignQuestions.tradeOffs: Type 3 on country keeps the dimension compact and queries simple but discards older country history. Type 2 on loyalty_tier preserves full history at the cost of row growth and more complex queries. Mixing types on one dimension increases ETL complexity but matches each attribute's actual requirements.
systemDesignQuestions.scalingStrategy: Index the natural key for fast change detection, use set-based MERGE for both Type 2 and Type 3 logic, partition the Type 2 history by effective_date for large volumes, and stream change events to an audit log so Type 3's discarded history is still recoverable if requirements change.

Why is IS DISTINCT FROM preferred over a simple <> comparison in the change-detection clause?

Can Type 3 support point-in-time attribution of historical facts? Why or why not?

cheatSheet.oneLineDefinition: SCD Type 3 tracks limited history by adding extra columns (current + previous value) on the same row instead of inserting new rows.
keyConcepts: Limited history: only a fixed number of prior values are kept.
Column shift: on change, current value moves to previous, new value becomes current.
Constant row count: one row per natural key, no row explosion.
Lossy: older history beyond the retained columns is discarded.
Effective_date: records when the current value took effect.
commands: CREATE TABLE dim (... current_region VARCHAR, previous_region VARCHAR, region_effective_date DATE ...);
UPDATE d SET previous_region = d.current_region, current_region = s.region, region_effective_date = CURRENT_DATE FROM dim d JOIN stg s ON d.nk = s.nk WHERE d.current_region IS DISTINCT FROM s.region;
INSERT new keys with previous_region = NULL when no matching dimension row exists.
interviewPoints: Type 3 = limited history via columns; Type 2 = full history via rows; Type 1 = overwrite, no history.
On change: shift current -> previous, write new -> current, set effective_date.
Lossy and schema-rigid; poor fit for frequently changing attributes.
Guard the shift with IS DISTINCT FROM for idempotency.
Use for current-vs-previous comparison (e.g., territory realignment); graduate to Type 2 / Type 6 for full history.
quickNotes: Type 3 keeps exactly one row per natural key; queries need no window functions or date-range joins.
Only the most recent N prior values survive; the rest are overwritten permanently.
Adding history depth or tracking a new attribute's prior value requires a DDL schema change.
Re-shifting unchanged rows is the classic corruption bug — always compare staged vs current first.
Hybrid Type 6 (1+2+3) combines full Type 2 history with Type 3-style current-vs-prior comparison columns.

keyTakeaways: SCD Type 3 tracks limited history by adding extra columns (e.g., current_region and previous_region) and keeps exactly one row per natural key — it adds columns, not rows.
On change, the old current value is shifted into the previous column and the new value becomes current, optionally stamped with an effective_date; older history is permanently discarded.
It is purpose-built for current-vs-previous comparison (like sales territory realignment) where full history is overkill, giving compact dimensions and simple queries.
Its core limitations are lossy history, schema rigidity, and unsuitability for frequently changing or audit-critical attributes — use Type 2 (or hybrid Type 6) when full history is required.
Make Type 3 loads idempotent by guarding the column shift with IS DISTINCT FROM so replays never overwrite the genuine prior value.
